[Daniel A. Brent]{.name}

[Associate Professor · Department of Agricultural Economics, Sociology, & Education · Penn State University]{.role}

[Email](mailto:dab320@psu.edu){.btn-link} [CV (PDF)](assets/cv/DanielBrentCV.pdf){.btn-link} [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=-0oqdtsAAAAJ&hl=en){.btn-link} [GitHub](https://github.com/dbrentecon){.btn-link}

Dr. Brent is an applied microeconomist whose research sits at the intersection of environmental economics, water resource economics, behavioral economics, and public policy analysis. He is currently an Associate Professor in the Department of Agricultural Economics, Sociology, & Education at Pennsylvania State University. Dr. Brent’s research focuses on understanding how economic agents respond to incentives, environmental stimuli, and information in settings with externalities. His work uses field experiments, behavioral economics, quasi-experimental variation, and machine learning to address pressing environmental and resource challenges. Recent projects examine peer effects in voluntary environmental programs, the frictions in water assistance programs, the introduction of volumetric water pricing, and the interaction between behavioral nudges and economic incentives. Another strand of his work studies financial literacy and cost misperceptions in higher education.

Dr. Brent currently teaches a PhD econometrics course on causal inference and an undergraduate personal finance course. Prior teaching includes environmental economics, principles of microeconomics, and intermediate microeconomics.
:::

## Teaching {#teaching}

My teaching emphasizes rigorous causal reasoning applied to real-world policy questions. Across graduate and undergraduate courses, I focus on helping students develop intuition for identification, connect theory to data, and implement modern empirical methods using reproducible workflows in R. I also teach personal finance which implants practical skills for navigating complex financial decisions.

::: {.course-grid}

::: {.course}
[PhD · EEFE 530]{.course-tag}

**Causal Inference and Applied Econometrics**

Potential outcomes, identification, randomized and quasi-experimental designs, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, panel methods, and threats to validity. Implemented in R with reproducible, replication-oriented workflows (R, Quarto, GitHub; administrative and experimental data).
:::

::: {.course}
[Undergraduate]{.course-tag}

**Personal Financial Decision-Making**

Budgeting, credit, student loans, investing, insurance, and retirement planning, with an emphasis on evidence-based decision-making and long-term financial wellbeing.
:::

::: {.course}
[Undergraduate]{.course-tag}

**Environmental Economics and Policy**

Economic analysis of environmental and natural resource issues, including externalities, public goods, climate change, and environmental regulation.
:::

::: {.course}
[Undergraduate]{.course-tag}

**Economic Analysis of Environmental and Resource Policies**

Benefit–cost analysis, policy evaluation, and empirical evidence in environmental and resource economics.
:::

:::

**Previous teaching.** *Louisiana State University:* Environmental Economics; Intermediate Microeconomic Theory; Principles of Microeconomics. *University of Washington:* Intermediate Microeconomics; Introductory Microeconomics.

**Advising.** I advise PhD and MS students on applied research in environmental economics, water resources, and causal inference. I am especially interested in projects that combine field experiments, administrative data, and policy evaluation.
